particulars: All names (victim initials, the two teenagers, analyst, defense and appellate lawyers, reporters, experts, DA, governor, the actual perpetrators), the Houston/Harris and Fort Bend County setting, the 1998–2007 dates, the ages, heights and weights, the 1-in-694,000 and 1-in-15/1-in-8 statistics, the 25-year sentence, the $600 fee and the $118,000 compensation plus $1,700 annuity are absent.

items.record: The case is a criminal prosecution for rape: a teenager was convicted, imprisoned and later exonerated: "Josiah Sutton was convicted on July 9, 1999, and sentenced to 25 years in prison."
items.reading: Guesses at scattered complaints about health effects, benefit denials or safety, handled by a regulator or ministry.
items.loss: The basic kind of event and the domain it belongs to.

items.record: The text is a narrative account of a wrongful conviction, not a document produced by the institution in question: "Separately, two reporters with KHOU-TV... had begun investigating the Houston crime lab."
items.reading: An official findings report written by the implicated state body for its own archive, framing matters as closed.
items.loss: Who wrote the text and from which side of the dispute.

items.record: The harm came from an eyewitness identification at a show-up despite clear physical mismatch: "Josiah was about 6 inches taller and 60 pounds heavier than P.S.' description."
items.loss: The first mechanism that produced the wrongful accusation.

items.record: A crime lab produced flawed DNA analysis, mistyped the victim's sample and misreported an exculpatory sample: "The lab report had erroneously stated that DNA types consistent with Mr. Sutton were found on this sample, when in fact, he had been excluded."
items.reading: Statements are 'probably accurate, relevant and properly sourced'; the illusion comes only from framing, 'not from any lie.'
items.loss: Whether the institutional record contained real factual errors or was merely narrowly framed.

items.record: The statistic given to the jury hugely overstated the match. With two suspects the real chance was better than 1 in 8: "this is the statistic that the jury needed in order to assign proper meaning to the DNA 'match.'"
items.loss: How misleading numbers turned weak evidence into apparent certainty.

items.record: Defense counsel failed the accused. He never authorized the paid independent test, hired no expert and opened the door to past convictions: "Well, I'm sorry, man, but that's what they came up with."
items.loss: The failure of the person who was supposed to protect the accused.

items.record: The prosecutor actively cut off testimony about the exculpatory sample: "I don't want to talk about the unknown sample, okay?"
items.reading: Suppression by passive procedural narrowing in an after-the-fact report.
items.loss: Where and how suppression happened: live, in court, by a specific actor at trial.

items.record: The appeals court relied on the flawed evidence itself to reject the appeal: "The State's DNA evidence... is not seriously challenged."
items.loss: The circular step where the error shielded itself from review.

items.record: The breakthrough came through a chain of outsiders: defense attorneys' tip, reporters, independent experts, and the mother who saw the broadcast and called the station: "Mr. Sutton's mother, Carol Batie, caught the story on television and called the station."
items.reading: Vaguely suggests 'media attention, litigation or online organizing' as escalation, and leaves the driver unknown.
items.loss: The specific sequence of people and links that reopened the case.

items.record: The convicted man acted for himself from prison by drafting his own motion under a statute that did not strictly apply, which led to appointed counsel.
items.reading: Affected people are isolated, doubting themselves and possibly erased.
items.loss: The individual's own agency in starting his exoneration.

items.record: The case was resolved. Retesting excluded him, he was released and pardoned for innocence, compensated, and the true perpetrator was later identified through CODIS and pleaded guilty.
items.reading: 'It probably does not resolve'; the record later becomes evidence in a reckoning.
items.loss: The actual outcome and the vindication of the accused.

items.record: Even after exclusion the prosecution resisted, demanding further testing, declining to back an innocence pardon because the victim had not recanted, and opposing habeas: "The prosecution still declined to support a pardon based on innocence."
items.loss: The institution's continued resistance after its error was exposed, and the grounds it gave.

items.record: Race and youth shaped the case. Young Black teenagers were picked up on the street, and the match statistics were framed by racial population: "1 in 694,000 Black persons."
items.reading: A scattered 'marginal group' with no collective voice, demographics unknown.
items.loss: Who the affected people were and why they were vulnerable.

items.record: The co-accused was released after DNA excluded him, which made the remaining defendant look more surely guilty to the court.
items.loss: How the outcome for one accused person shaped the case against the other.
